title: Apparent free will stems from irreducible brain computation

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Apparent free will stems from irreducible brain computation

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The apparent freedom of human will arises because, although brain components follow definite laws, the brain's overall behavior is an irreducible computation whose outcome cannot be found by reasonable laws; no external influence, chaos, or quantum randomness is needed.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: even though all the components of our brains presumably follow definite laws, I strongly suspect that their overall behavior corresponds to an irreducible computation whose outcome can never in effect be found by reasonable laws.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “The Phenomenon of Free Will” (from p. 750), p. 750. Scope: human brains and other systems that appear to exhibit free will

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-19: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.23

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing neuroscience data may test local predictability but cannot resolve the claimed origin of apparent freedom. Every plausible observation remains compatible with several rival mechanisms, making the central explanatory claim non-discriminating.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: A proxy study could compare predictability of neural dynamics with reported agency, but no agreed measurement maps apparent freedom to computational irreducibility or separates this explanation from chaos, noise, and incomplete observation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Free will and reasonable laws lack operational definitions.

Neural unpredictability does not identify its computational cause.

The necessary complete brain state and dynamics are unavailable.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The hypothesis is about brains: component laws are definite, overall behavior is an irreducible computation, and chaos, quantum randomness, and external influence are unnecessary. Connectomes and brain atlases record structure and some activity. They do not record a closed dynamical law on which a search for predictive shortcuts could be run, so the decisive comparison is not available yet.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Given a mechanistic model of brain dynamics, compare the cost of predicting behavior from that model with the cost of stepping the model, and test whether the unpredictability survives without chaotic amplification or quantum randomness. A compact predictive law would refute irreducibility; current atlases do not contain that model.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Reasonable laws and apparent freedom still need an explicit criterion.

Whole-brain mechanistic dynamics at the resolution needed to search for shortcuts are not a public dataset.

Chaos, quantum noise, and external drive remain available alternative accounts.
